newsitem.title: FRANCE: Prince Charles gets pop star welcome in Paris.
newsitem.headline: Prince Charles gets pop star welcome in Paris.

text.p: Britain's Prince Charles received a noisy pop star's welcome on Thursday when he visited three troubled, heavily immigrant-populated suburbs of Paris.

"Charleee...Charleee," shouted hundreds of excited teenagers, nearly all of North African Arab or black African origin, as he toured the sprawling council estates of Dugny, Clichy-sous-Bois and Aulnay-sous-Bois.

The heir to the throne, who heads several British bodies involved in urban regeneration and youth activities, was returning a visit to Glasgow's giant Easter estate by French President Jacques Chirac last May.
"He's interested in the French poor. Why are the French not interested in the French poor?" asked 15-year-old Ali, complaining that French Prime Minister Alain Juppe was not present.

The prince was accompanied by Eric Raoult, junior Minister for Urban Affairs and Integration and a key force behind a government drive to integrate about four million foreigners and 1.7 million of their local-born children into French society.
Immigration, an explosive issue in France, has fuelled the rise of extreme right-wing leader Jean-Marie Pen who wants to expell all foreigners.
"The problem is unemployment," said Robert Labuthie, a local official at Clichy-sous-Bois. "About 40 percent of adults here are out of work.
"Since more than half the population is under 25 and has virtually no hope of employment after school, that spells big trouble."

Nervous riot policemen with heavy truncheons at their belts hovered in the background, but there were no incidents as the prince toured urban renewal projects and called greetings to hundreds of small children cheerily waving hand-painted Union Jacks.

He visited the impeccable flat of Amara Hadboun, an Algerian-born mother of nine in traditional garb who speaks no French despite living in France since 1954. Her children were cited as models of successful integration as several of the girls became nurses.
"I am very impressed by the French experience (in urban renewal and other projects). We must learn to work together," the prince later told reporters.
A delighted Raoult said the visit showed "there are other things Europe can turn its attention to besides monetary matters."

Perhaps the only Frenchman of European origin in the crowd at Clichy-sous-Bois, in the shadow of delapidated high rise council flats, was 78-year-old Raymond Denis. He wore medals showing he served with General Charles de Gaulle's Free French forces in World War Two.
"I'd like to thank the prince for the welcome the British people gave us during the war, for arming us and allowing us to help liberate France with them," he said.
But the old paratrooper was swept aside in the crush as the crowd surged forward shouting: "Monsieur le Prince," "Monsieur le Prince."
